opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's one of the most fundamental problems, and it's interesting because it shows up in both settings, just in slightly different forms.

At the core, both Veo and Genie are trying to generate a sequence of frames that feels like it comes from a coherent world. When you watch a video, your brain is very sensitive to things that don't hold together. An object changes color, a character's face drifts a bit, a building that was on the left is suddenly gone when the camera pans back. Those are consistency failures, and people notice them immediately, even if each individual frame looks great.

With video generation, there's a big structural advantage: the model generates the whole clip, or large chunks of it, at once. It can attend across the entire time window and make sure the beginning and the end agree with each other. So consistency is mostly about the model learning good enough representations of the world, of objects, of physics, that everything lines up within that window.

With an interactive world model like Genie, it's much harder, because you're generating frame by frame, or chunk by chunk, in real time, conditioned on actions the user takes that you couldn't anticipate. You don't get to see the future. And the user can go anywhere. They can walk away from something, turn around a minute later, and expect it to still be there, looking the same. So now consistency isn't just about a few seconds of coherence. It's about memory. The model has to keep some representation of what it has already generated and stay faithful to it over a long horizon, while still being fast enough to respond to inputs.

What I find really interesting is that we didn't build an explicit 3D representation for that. There's no mesh, no scene graph. The consistency, to the extent it works, emerges from training. The model learns that the world is persistent because the data it sees is from a persistent world. That's powerful, because it generalizes in ways an explicit representation might not, but it also means you're relying on the model to learn the right thing, and errors can accumulate over time.

So I'd say the shared challenge is building a model that really has an internal understanding of a world that persists. Video generation tests that over a bounded window where the model sees everything. Interactive world models push it much further: longer horizons, no lookahead, real-time constraints, and a user actively probing the edges. In a sense, progress on one helps the other, because better world understanding in video models gives you a stronger foundation, and the interactive setting is a very unforgiving test of whether that understanding is actually there.

r001.rationale: It describes a building disappearing when the camera pans back as a consistency failure and says a user expects a scene to persist after turning around.

r002.rationale: It does not mention an early Doom-based next-frame model or attribute short-context performance to memorizing the level layout.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the way I'd frame it is that consistency is really the same underlying problem in both cases, it just shows up with different constraints.

In a video generator like Veo, the model gets to see the whole clip it's producing. It's generating all the frames, or at least a big chunk of them, jointly, so it can reason about the beginning and the end at the same time. If a character walks behind a pillar and comes back out, the model has the full temporal context to make sure the same character emerges. Consistency there is largely about the model having a strong enough internal representation of the scene, the objects, the physics, so that what it produces is coherent across time and across viewpoints.

With an interactive world model like Genie, you lose that luxury. The future isn't fixed, because the user is acting in the environment. You don't know what the person is going to do next, so you have to generate frame by frame, or a few frames at a time, and you're always conditioning on what came before plus the action. That means consistency becomes a memory problem as much as a modeling problem. If you turn around, walk away for thirty seconds, and come back, the world should still be there the way you left it. That's hard, because the model has to carry forward a representation of things that are no longer visible, and it has to do that over long horizons without drift accumulating.

So I'd say the shared challenge is: does the model have a genuine, persistent understanding of the world it's rendering, rather than just producing plausible pixels locally? Veo makes that visible in the quality of the video. Genie makes it visible in whether the world holds together when you interact with it. And what's interesting is that progress on one tends to help the other. The same scaling, the same architectural improvements, the same emphasis on learning physical and spatial structure from video, show up as better long-range coherence in generation and as more stable, persistent worlds in the interactive setting. Fundamentally they're both asking the model to be a good simulator, and the interactive case just makes the gaps much more obvious.

r001.rationale: The response says the scene and objects should remain coherent “across time and across viewpoints,” which communicates visual consistency as the camera moves around the scene.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention an early Doom-based next-frame model, short context, or memorizing the game's level layout.

astra-6.text:
I think the shared challenge is that generating a plausible frame is different from generating a consistent world. You can have individual frames that look great, but as you move through the scene, objects change shape or disappear, or the layout stops making sense. The model needs to preserve information about things even when they’re not visible.

For video generation, that means maintaining coherence as the video unfolds. In an interactive world model, you have the additional challenge that the user determines what happens next. If you turn away from something and then turn back, you expect it to still be there. And if you take an action that changes it, you expect that change to persist.

So both require some understanding of an underlying world, rather than just what the next image should look like. Interactivity makes that requirement especially clear because the user can actively test whether the world is consistent.

r001.rationale: It says the scene should persist when the user turns away and back, directly conveying visual consistency as the camera moves.

r002.rationale: It does not mention the early Doom-based next-frame model, short context, or memorized level layout.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the shared challenge is that generating something plausible in a single frame is very different from generating a world that stays coherent over time. If an object moves out of view and then comes back, you expect it to be the same object. If you change something in the scene, you expect that change to persist. So the model needs to capture more than appearance—it needs some understanding of the underlying state and how that state evolves.

With video generation, you can judge that consistency along the sequence the model produces. In an interactive world model, the user can take actions that test it. You might turn around, revisit a location, or interact with an object in an unexpected way. The model has to respond to those actions while preserving what has already happened.

So there’s a common problem of temporal coherence, but interaction makes the requirement stronger. It’s not just, ‘Does this look like a convincing video?’ It’s, ‘Does this behave like a world I can keep interacting with?’

r001.rationale: The response says that turning around or revisiting a location should preserve the same world and object, conveying consistency as the camera moves through the scene.
